prompt_free_text:
This paper proposes a self-supervised EEG-text pretraining model, CET-MAE, that combines masked reconstruction for both modalities with EEG-text contrastive alignment, and then transfers the pretrained EEG-side components into an EEG-to-text generation framework, E2T-PTR, built around BART. The target application is open-vocabulary decoding from text-evoked EEG on ZuCo. The paper is timely and addresses an interesting problem at the intersection of multimodal representation learning, neural decoding, and language generation. The central intuition—that EEG-to-text decoding may benefit from jointly learning intra-modal reconstruction and cross-modal alignment before supervised fine-tuning—is reasonable and potentially valuable. The empirical results suggest modest but consistent gains over several prior baselines on ZuCo, and the paper includes a number of ablations.

Overall, I find the paper promising but not yet fully convincing at the level expected for a top-tier ML venue. The main concerns are around experimental rigor, fairness of comparisons, clarity of the task formulation, and the extent to which the reported gains can truly be attributed to the proposed pretraining rather than to changes in input construction, training scale, or evaluation protocol. The paper has good ideas, but the current presentation leaves several important ambiguities unresolved.

On the positive side, the paper’s main conceptual contribution is clear. CET-MAE combines three objectives: masked text modeling, masked EEG modeling, and EEG-text contrastive learning. This is a natural multimodal SSL design, and the multi-stream encoder is a plausible mechanism for balancing modality-specific and joint representations. The downstream transfer setup is also sensible: reuse the pretrained EEG encoder, projection layer, and EEG-stream transformer, then fine-tune jointly with BART for generation. The inclusion of sentence-level EEG as an additional token to compensate for missing word-level fixations is also practically motivated by the peculiarities of ZuCo. The paper further attempts to validate each ingredient through ablations over sentence-level EEG, pretraining, and masking ratios.

That said, the novelty should be calibrated carefully. Combining contrastive alignment with masked autoencoding is by itself not new; the novelty here is primarily the adaptation of this recipe to EEG-text pretraining for EEG-to-text decoding. That is a meaningful domain contribution, but the paper occasionally overstates its conceptual originality. For example, the claim of being “the first pre-trained EEG-text model for EEG-based language decoding” may be true in a narrow sense, but the broader methodological ingredients are established. The paper would be stronger if it framed its contribution more precisely as a domain-specific multimodal SSL instantiation and transfer study, rather than implying a fundamentally new learning paradigm.

The technical formulation is understandable at a high level, but several details are underspecified. It is not fully clear how the joint stream is constructed token-wise when EEG and text lengths differ, especially given missing word-level EEG due to absent fixations and the appended sentence-level EEG token. The paper says masked positions in the text stream are prevented from entering contrastive learning, but the exact masking and pooling behavior for contrastive loss is not sufficiently formalized. Likewise, the text side uses a frozen BART encoder during pretraining, but the downstream E2T-PTR fully fine-tunes BART; this asymmetry is acceptable, yet the rationale and its effect are not deeply analyzed. The decoder design for text reconstruction is also somewhat unusual: if BART already encodes masked tokens and positional information, and the text decoder is only a linear projection, then the burden of cross-modal reconstruction may be limited. More explicit equations and implementation details would help assess whether the model is truly learning rich cross-modal interactions or mostly leveraging strong pretrained text representations.

A major issue is the evaluation setup and fairness of comparisons. The paper compares against prior work across three, four, and five reading-task combinations, but the training sample counts differ across methods, and some baselines are reproduced while others are taken from prior papers. In Table 1, some comparisons are made at 10710 samples, others at 14407, others at 18791. This is understandable if prior work used different subsets, but it makes the headline “SOTA” claim less clean. More importantly, the gains over the strongest comparable baselines are relatively small in several settings. For example, under three reading tasks, E2T-PTR improves over DeWave from BLEU-4 8.22 to 8.99 and ROUGE-1 F from 30.69 to 32.61. These are nontrivial but modest gains, and no variance estimates or significance tests are reported. Given the small dataset and likely high variance in training generative models on EEG, reporting only single-run scores is insufficient. Confidence intervals or multiple-seed results are essential here.

The four-task comparison is even less convincing. Against C-SCL*, E2T-PTR is slightly better on BLEU-1/2 and ROUGE precision, but slightly worse on BLEU-3/4 and ROUGE recall/F1. Yet the abstract emphasizes outperforming the state of the art in ROUGE-1 F1 and BLEU-4 by large percentages. Those percentages appear to be relative improvements against selected baselines and selected settings, not a uniform dominance across all conditions. The paper should present a much more careful and transparent summary of where it wins, where it ties, and where it loses. As written, the framing overstates the empirical evidence.

Another concern is that multiple changes are bundled together in the downstream system: sentence-level EEG concatenation, CET-MAE pretraining, and the E2T-PTR transfer architecture. Table 5 partially disentangles these, which is good, but the improvements are again fairly small. From the no-sentence/no-pretraining setup to the full model, BLEU-4 rises from 7.68 to 8.99. This is meaningful, but it would be important to know how much of the gain comes simply from adding sentence-level EEG versus from the SSL objectives. The table suggests sentence-level EEG alone already gives a noticeable boost, and CET-MAE plus E2T-PTR adds further gains. However, there is no direct comparison against a strong baseline that also uses sentence-level EEG but no multimodal pretraining, under identical optimization and architecture choices. Without that, it is hard to isolate the true contribution of CET-MAE.

The treatment of “teacher forcing” is also problematic. The limitation section states that results still depend on the “implicit use of teacher forcing,” but this is not merely a minor caveat; it is central to interpreting the task. If the decoder is trained with teacher forcing and evaluated with standard autoregressive generation, that is normal. But if the task setup or preprocessing leaks target-side information beyond standard seq2seq training, that would be much more serious. The paper’s wording in Section 3.1—“During the testing phase, the model M operates with an implicit understanding of the ground-truth word tokens W”—is especially concerning and confusing. At test time, the model should not have any access, implicit or explicit, to ground-truth tokens except through standard decoding initialization. This sentence needs correction and clarification. As written, it raises doubts about the exact inference protocol.

Relatedly, the paper should discuss the extent to which the task is truly “decoding from EEG” versus “recovering text strongly constrained by the reading stimulus distribution.” ZuCo is text-evoked EEG during reading, not imagined speech or unconstrained language production. The model may exploit strong priors from the language model and dataset distribution, especially when sentence-level EEG is included and BART is fine-tuned. This does not invalidate the work, but it should temper claims about general brain-to-text decoding. The paper occasionally makes broad BCI claims that go beyond what the experiments support.

The qualitative examples are mixed. Some examples show improved grammaticality and phrase recovery, which is encouraging. However, many outputs still contain severe errors, hallucinations, and named-entity failures. In some five-task examples, the model reproduces long spans nearly exactly except for the first name or a verb, which suggests the language model prior is doing much of the work once enough context is inferred. This again underscores the need for stronger analyses beyond BLEU/ROUGE, such as content-word accuracy, named-entity accuracy, calibration against retrieval baselines, or comparisons to text-only priors conditioned on metadata or partial prompts. Otherwise it is difficult to assess what semantic information is genuinely extracted from EEG.

The masking-ratio analysis is interesting but not fully persuasive. The paper concludes that 75% masking is best, but the differences are tiny, and only one downstream setting is shown. Since the natural masking ratio in EEG is already high due to missing fixations, the effective corruption level becomes extreme. This could indeed encourage cross-modal reliance, but it could also simply regularize the model or force heavier dependence on the text branch during pretraining. A more informative analysis would report pretraining losses, reconstruction quality, and downstream transfer under multiple seeds, or compare compulsory masking of sentence-level EEG against optional masking. As it stands, the explanation is plausible but speculative.

The paper also lacks several important baselines and controls. First, a text-only or language-model prior baseline would be useful: for example, generating from BART conditioned only on sentence length or task identity, or from a null EEG embedding, to quantify how much of the score comes from language priors. Second, an EEG-only SSL baseline not involving text, such as MAEEG-style pretraining transferred into the same E2T-PTR architecture, would help determine whether cross-modal pretraining is actually necessary. The paper cites prior EEG-only pretraining work but does not compare directly in the same downstream framework. Third, a simpler multimodal alignment baseline, such as CLIP-style contrastive pretraining without the joint stream or without text reconstruction, should be compared more thoroughly than the small CET/ET-MAE table. The gains in Table 6 are quite small, so significance matters.

There are also reproducibility and reporting issues. Key implementation details appear deferred to appendices not included here, but for a top-tier review I would want explicit information on subject splits, whether splits are sentence-disjoint across subjects, how hyperparameters were selected, whether validation data was used for model selection, and whether any test-set tuning occurred. Since ZuCo is small and heterogeneous across tasks and subjects, leakage risks are real. The paper says it follows Wang and Ji’s preprocessing and splits, which helps, but more explicit confirmation is needed. It would also be useful to know computational cost, parameter counts, and whether the pretrained text encoder being frozen during SSL but unfrozen downstream materially affects results.

The writing is generally understandable but uneven. There are numerous grammatical issues, repeated claims, and some imprecise statements. The paper would benefit from substantial editing for clarity and precision. Examples include the confusing test-time description noted above, inconsistent terminology around “LLMs” versus BART, and occasional overclaiming such as “our experiments are the most comprehensive” without a clearly defined criterion. The ethics statement is also too brief. Even if no new human data were collected, brain decoding work has obvious privacy implications, and the statement should acknowledge potential misuse and the limits of current systems.

In terms of significance, I do think the paper addresses an important direction. Multimodal SSL for neural signal decoding is underexplored, and EEG-text pretraining is a reasonable and potentially impactful idea. The empirical gains, while modest, suggest the approach may be useful. However, the current evidence does not yet fully establish that the proposed method is a robust advance rather than an incremental improvement aided by architectural and input modifications. For acceptance at a top-tier ML conference, I would expect stronger experimental controls, clearer inference protocol description, statistical rigor, and more careful claims.

My main suggestions for improvement are as follows. First, clarify the exact test-time decoding protocol and remove any wording that suggests access to ground-truth text at inference. Second, report mean and standard deviation over multiple random seeds, and ideally significance tests against the strongest baselines. Third, add stronger controls: a no-EEG or null-EEG baseline, an EEG-only SSL pretraining baseline transferred into the same downstream architecture, and a sentence-level-EEG-only architectural control without multimodal pretraining. Fourth, provide more detailed analyses of what information is decoded from EEG, such as content-word accuracy, named-entity accuracy, or performance stratified by word frequency and part of speech. Fifth, better disentangle the contributions of sentence-level EEG concatenation, contrastive learning, and masked reconstruction. Sixth, moderate the claims about SOTA and about general BCI implications, especially given the text-evoked reading setting.

In summary, this is an interesting and potentially useful paper with a sensible multimodal SSL idea and encouraging results on ZuCo. Its strengths are the relevance of the problem, the coherent pretraining-transfer framework, and the inclusion of several ablations. Its weaknesses are insufficiently rigorous evaluation, unclear fairness in comparisons, modest gains without uncertainty estimates, and some ambiguity in task formulation and inference. I would currently lean borderline to weak reject for a top-tier ML venue, mainly because the empirical evidence and presentation do not yet match the ambition of the claims. With stronger experimental validation and clearer exposition, this line of work could become a solid contribution.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper proposes CET-MAE, a multimodal self-supervised pretraining framework for EEG-text representation learning that combines masked reconstruction for both modalities with EEG-text contrastive alignment via a multi-stream transformer. It then introduces E2T-PTR, which transfers the pretrained EEG-side components into an EEG-to-text generation system built on BART. Experiments on ZuCo reading-task combinations report improvements over prior EEG-to-text methods on BLEU and ROUGE metrics, along with ablations on masking ratios, sentence-level EEG inclusion, and alternative SSL objectives.
strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: open-vocabulary EEG-to-text decoding from non-invasive recordings.
The proposed pretraining objective is intuitively motivated, combining cross-modal contrastive alignment with intra-modal masked reconstruction.
The paper includes several ablations: masking ratios, inclusion of sentence-level EEG features, and comparisons among CET, ET-MAE, and CET-MAE.
Use of both word-level and sentence-level EEG features is a reasonable design choice for mitigating missing fixation-aligned word EEG.
Empirical results show consistent but modest gains over reproduced baselines on several settings, especially in the three-task and five-task setups.
weaknesses: The empirical gains over the strongest comparable methods are often small in absolute terms, and no statistical significance tests or variance across runs are reported, making it unclear whether improvements are robust.

Fairness of comparisons is questionable: some baselines use different training sample counts, some are reproduced by the authors while others are taken from prior work, and evaluation conventions differ (e.g., repeated-word handling).

The paper acknowledges reliance on teacher forcing / implicit access to target tokens, which substantially weakens the claim of practical EEG-to-text decoding and raises concerns about how much of the performance comes from language-model priors rather than EEG information.

Methodological details are insufficient for reproducibility and interpretation: exact contrastive loss formulation, pooling strategy details, masking implementation, subject split protocol, and how sentence-level EEG is aligned and injected are not fully specified in the main text.

The claimed novelty is overstated; combining contrastive learning and masked autoencoding is established in multimodal SSL, and the paper mainly adapts these ideas to EEG-text rather than introducing a fundamentally new learning principle.
Qualitative examples reveal that outputs remain heavily driven by generic language patterns and struggle with named entities, suggesting limited true semantic decoding from EEG.
The paper makes broad claims about advancing BCI applications, but the current setup is restricted to text-evoked reading data from ZuCo and does not demonstrate realistic communication decoding.
There is no analysis of subject generalization, calibration requirements, or robustness across tasks/subjects, which are central for EEG-based BCIs.
methodological_flaws: A major scientific validity concern is the use of teacher forcing / implicit ground-truth token access during decoding. If target-side information is available during training/evaluation in a way comparable to prior work, the reported generation quality may substantially reflect conditional language modeling rather than EEG decoding ability. This should be isolated with stricter inference protocols and stronger baselines.

The comparison protocol is not fully controlled. Results are reported across different dataset sizes (10710, 14407, 18791), with some baselines reproduced and others copied from prior papers, and with alternate metric computation conventions (retaining repeated words or not). This undermines causal attribution of gains to the proposed method.

No confidence intervals, standard deviations, or multi-seed results are provided despite very small absolute improvements in many tables (e.g., tenths of a BLEU point). Without uncertainty estimates, claims of superiority are not empirically well supported.

The paper claims that sentence-level EEG acts as data augmentation and alleviates semantic discrepancy, but this is not rigorously validated. Since sentence-level EEG may encode broad contextual information correlated with the target sentence, concatenating it could change the task substantially and may leak high-level sentence identity cues relative to word-level decoding baselines.

The masking-ratio conclusions are based on limited trial-and-error settings and only downstream BLEU, without analyzing pretraining loss behavior or representation quality. The argument that 75% masking is optimal is therefore weakly supported.

The mathematical presentation is minimal and incomplete: the contrastive objective is not explicitly defined, negative sampling strategy is unspecified, and there is no formal justification for the multi-stream architecture or for excluding masked learnable vectors from the text stream beyond intuition.

The paper does not disentangle gains from pretraining versus gains from architectural changes and additional sentence-level inputs. Although ablations exist, they do not fully isolate whether improvements come from CET-MAE, from E2T-PTR design changes, or simply from more informative inputs and stronger fine-tuning of BART.
